body: A bank card, held edge-on, smears ice about as much as it clears it, but the scraper went missing in November and this is what there is. Ten to seven on a Tuesday morning, and a man in a high-visibility coat works along the windscreen of a twelve-seat minibus outside a community hall. There are four people to collect and three hospital appointments between them, and one of the four will not be ready. He knows which one. In the door pocket there is a bag of boiled sweets, which he started buying in his second week after somebody was sick, and a folder of route notes that nobody has ever asked to see. He has been doing this for three years. He volunteered once, for one week, as a favour.

Nobody appointed him and there was no moment of decision. He said yes to a fortnight, the fortnight ended, and the job simply stayed attached to him. If you asked him what his purpose was he would look at you oddly and say that somebody has to drive the bus.

The modern version of that question is introspective. What am I passionate about, what am I good at, what would I do if money were no object — and somewhere in the overlap of those three the answer is supposed to be waiting. It is a search, conducted inward, and the person searching is also the one who decides when it has succeeded.

It would be cheap to sneer at that. People reach for this material because something has genuinely gone missing. A great deal of modern work is abstract: it produces a number that goes into a system, and the good it does, if it does any, happens somewhere the worker never sees. Then there is the mobility. A man who inherits his father’s trade never has to ask what he is for, because the answer was in the house. Take away the trade, the place and the expectation, tell a person that any life is available to them, and you have handed them a genuinely difficult question along with the freedom. The find-your-purpose shelf exists because that question is real and nobody else was answering it.

There is a frequency set aside for the subject on this band. HM 384.50 — Purpose Found — is assigned and in build, not yet on air, still silent. The dial itself runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, of which 46 are on air today.

What the shelf cannot do is the part that costs something, because almost nobody in Scripture discovers their purpose. It is handed to them, usually while they are busy with something else, and usually unwelcome. Taking that seriously has a price, and the price is that you stop auditioning. You do not get to hold the current work at arm’s length as a placeholder until the real thing turns up. You have to do the unremarkable job in front of you as though it might be the assignment, for years, without the compensation of knowing.

That is an unfashionable thing to ask of anybody now, and the reason is not that people have become shallow. It is that the self has become the last available authority. Institutions that used to hand out roles are distrusted, and what is left is the individual and their own sense of fit. So the question gets turned inward by default, and an entire industry grows up to help with the excavation — the assessment, the retreat, the workbook with the three overlapping circles. Almost none of it is fraudulent. It is simply doing archaeology on the one site that cannot contain what is being looked for.

Look at how the assignments actually arrive in the text, because the pattern is remarkably consistent. Moses is minding a flock on the back side of the desert and spends most of the conversation explaining why he is the wrong man. Gideon is threshing wheat in a winepress, hiding, and argues. Amos is explicit that he was no prophet and no prophet’s son but a herdsman, and that he was taken from following the flock. Jonah receives an unusually clear brief and books passage in the opposite direction. Not one of them was searching. Every one of them was occupied.
The consistent feature in those accounts is not enthusiasm. It is that somebody else decided.

The fair objection is that gifts are real, and the shelf is not wrong about that. Scripture takes it for granted that people are differently made and differently equipped, and it never suggests that a person should ignore what they can plainly do. Somebody miserable in work that wastes them is not being more spiritual by staying there. But notice what the search can and cannot produce. It can return an inventory of what is already in you. It cannot hand you anything, because there is nobody in that room to do the handing, and a purpose has to come from outside the person if it is to make any claim on them at all.
A purpose you award yourself is not an assignment. It is a preference with better lighting.

It is twenty past two in the morning and a woman is behind the counter of a petrol station, sitting on a stool she is not supposed to sit on, working through the coffee machine cleaning cycle because the shift is long. A lorry driver comes in for a sandwich and does not leave. He tells her about his brother, who is in hospital in another county, and about a phone call he did not return in September. She says almost nothing. She knows the sandwich is going cold and she lets it go cold. When he finally goes she wipes the counter he has been leaning on, and she does not think about any of it again until the following Thursday when a different man does more or less the same thing.

She has not been assigned a ministry. But the work found her at the counter, at an hour she did not choose, in a job she took because it fitted around her mother — which is the entire pattern, arriving exactly where it always arrives.

It is only honest to say that this is worse news than the shelf offers, in one specific way. An assignment you did not choose is frequently uninteresting and often thankless. People spend decades on work that nobody admires. And the text is not sentimental about this either: several of the people who received the clearest assignments in Scripture had their lives comprehensively ruined by them, and said so at length, and were not talked out of it.

But the difficulty is not a defect in the arrangement. It is the arrangement, and it is what makes the thing worth having. A purpose that has been assigned does not depend on how you feel about it on a wet Tuesday in February, which is precisely when a self-selected one collapses. It survives your boredom. It survives your doubts about whether you are the right person, because you were never the one who decided that, and the argument about your suitability is with somebody else and was settled without you.

So the advice, such as it is, runs backwards from the usual. Stop excavating yourself for a calling that was never buried in there. Do the work that is actually in front of you, keep turning up where you have said you would, and stay findable — because in every one of those accounts, the assignment turned up exactly where the person already was, doing something ordinary. The bus still needs driving at ten to seven. That is not a consolation prize for people who never found their purpose. That is what the finding looks like from the inside.
All of which is theory until ten to seven tomorrow morning. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial carries four kinds of programming and it is worth knowing they are there. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, gospel, hymns, country. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe: entertaining, clean, and playable in a room with children in it whether or not every track names God out loud. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages for the nations rather than translated into them afterwards. Four kinds, one dial, and no menu to work through to reach them.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 310.90 — Latin Worship, which runs in English and Spanish together. It is the frequency on this dial that most stubbornly refuses to consult you. It will not ask which language you would like the next three minutes in, and about half the time the answer will be one you do not have. That is the recommendation, and it follows from everything above: a station that hands you what it is playing is doing to your afternoon exactly what this article says happens to a life. It is also, as it happens, music made largely by working people in rooms with the chairs pushed back — sung by people who were not asked what they were passionate about first, and who turned up anyway.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are really reaching for, which is how the next station gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Do not audition it. Put HM 310.90 on tomorrow while you are doing the job you already have, and let it play the songs it was going to play anyway. You will not have chosen them, you will not understand a fair number of them, and one of them will get into you somewhere between the kettle and the car — which is more or less how everything important has ever arrived.
